content.title: About
content.content: Burrito with pork, beans, and cheese is a Mexican dish consisting of a large soft tortilla filled with sautéed pork, cooked beans, shredded cheese, and often topped with salsa, sour cream, or guacamole.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Burritos originated in northern Mexico, where tortillas served as a convenient “container” for meals on the go.
Pork in traditional burritos is often marinated with spices such as cumin, chili, and oregano for a rich flavor.
Beans, usually black or pinto, provide a valuable source of plant‑based protein and fiber.
Shredded cheese, commonly cheddar or Mexican “queso,” melts to create a creamy texture and enhance taste.
Burritos are frequently served with a wedge of lime, adding fresh acidity that balances the richness of the pork.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pork and beans supply high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Iron source
items.content: Pork provides heme iron, which is more readily absorbed, while beans add non‑heme iron.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: Beans are rich in soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium and small amounts of vitamin D, important for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both pork and beans contain B1, B6, and niacin, which are vital for energy metabolism.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Pork and cheese can be high in saturated fat; people with cardiovascular concerns should watch portion size.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared sauces and cheese often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Burritos are calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Burritos are usually served hot, cut in half, and eaten with hands or with a fork and knife. Add salsa, guacamole, or sour cream to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked burritos in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze; thaw before reheating and warm in an oven or microwave.

content.title: About
content.content: Candy “Cotton” is a soft sweet coated with a sugar glaze and filled with an airy cotton‑like mousse. The product is made from sugar, glucose syrup, flavorings and food colourings. It has a gentle sweet taste and a light texture reminiscent of marshmallow.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cotton‑filled candies first appeared in the United States in the 1970s.
The name “Cotton” refers to the visual similarity of the mousse to cotton fibers.
In Russia these candies are often sold in brightly coloured packets, making them popular with children.
The airy mousse is created by a foaming process similar to that used for marshmallows.
Cotton candies are frequently used as decorative elements for desserts and cakes.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: The sugar in the candy is rapidly absorbed, providing an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Sweet taste stimulates serotonin production, which can temporarily lift mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Allergy to food additives
items.content: Some versions may contain flavourings or colourings that can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Not suitable for young children
items.content: The soft texture can pose a choking hazard for small children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Candy “Cotton” can be enjoyed as a standalone sweet snack, used as a garnish for ice cream, cakes and desserts, or added to drinks to give an airy texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the candy in a dry, cool place in an airtight package protected from direct sunlight. For longer storage, keep it in the refrigerator to prevent the glaze from melting.

content.title: About
content.content: Iced latte is a cold coffee beverage made with espresso, cold milk, and ice. It blends the strength of coffee with the smoothness of milk, creating a refreshing drink popular in warm weather.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Iced latte originated in Japan in the 1990s as a variation of the classic latte.
A double shot of espresso is often used so the coffee flavor remains strong after dilution with ice.
Many countries add flavor syrups such as vanilla, caramel, or fruit extracts.
Cold‑brew coffee can be used in iced latte to reduce bitterness.
Ice cubes are usually large to melt slowly and avoid over‑diluting the drink.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Caffeine in espresso stimulates the central nervous system, improving alertness and reducing fatigue.

items.title: Antioxidant source
items.content: Coffee contains polyphenols that help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Caffeine may slightly increase metabolic rate, aiding calorie burning.

items.title: Calcium from milk
items.content: Milk provides calcium essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Although coffee has a mild diuretic effect, a cold latte still contributes to daily fluid intake.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: People sensitive to caffeine may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Sweet syrups can make the drink high‑calorie and promote weight gain.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Those who cannot digest lactose should use plant‑based milks such as almond, soy, or oat.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can increase stomach acidity, causing discomfort for individuals with gastritis or reflux.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve iced latte in tall glasses with a straw. It can be topped with whipped cream, a sprinkle of cinnamon, or a drizzle of flavored syrup. For a lighter version, use skim or plant‑based milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Brewed espresso can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Milk should remain sealed in its original container. Ice should be made from clean water and changed every 2–3 days to prevent off‑flavors.

content.title: About
content.content: Meat loaf made with venison is a baked loaf of ground deer meat mixed with eggs, breadcrumbs, spices, and sometimes vegetables. Venison offers a rich, slightly sweet flavor and low fat content, making the loaf both hearty and aromatic.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Venison is considered a "lean" meat: it contains less fat and fewer calories than beef.
Traditional venison meat loaves have been prepared in northern Europe and North America where deer were a primary meat source.
Deer meat is high in iron and zinc, making it a valuable food for energy and immune support.
Recipes often include fragrant herbs such as rosemary, thyme, and sage to highlight the natural game flavor.
A cooked venison meat loaf can be refrigerated for up to 4 days and frozen for up to 3 months without quality loss.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Venison provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with beef, venison has less saturated fat, which is beneficial for heart health.

items.title: High iron content
items.content: The iron in venison is readily absorbed and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Source of zinc and B‑vitamins
items.content: Zinc supports immunity, while B6 and B12 vitamins are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: A slice of venison meat loaf provides satiety without excessive calories.

items.title: Game meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to deer meat.

items.title: Parasite risk
items.content: Improper cooking can leave parasites in the meat; ensure the loaf is fully cooked.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Venison is rich in purines, which may be problematic for people with gout.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Certain recipes use a lot of salt or preservatives; monitor their amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the venison meat loaf hot as a main dish, slice thinly for sandwiches, add to salads, or use as a hearty accompaniment to soups. It pairs well with mustard, cranberry sauce, or a light yogurt dip.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked loaf in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions; thaw in the fridge and reheat in the oven before serving.

mustard-greens-frozen-cooked-no-added-fa.title: Mustard greens, frozen, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Mustard greens (Brassica juncea) are a leafy cruciferous vegetable rich in vitamins and minerals. In the frozen form they are blanched and flash‑frozen, preserving most of their nutrients. The product is ready to eat without any added fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mustard greens belong to the Brassicaceae family, the same as broccoli and cabbage.
Their leaves have been used in Asian cuisine and traditional medicine for centuries.
Quick blanching before freezing locks in the bright green color and a crisp texture.
The raw leaves have a mildly peppery bite that mellows with cooking.
In the United States they are a staple in Southern cooking and often appear in salads.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K supports blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: High in vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in mustard greens promotes eye health and immune function.

items.title: Good source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C provides antioxidant protection and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low in calories and fat
items.content: One cup of cooked mustard greens contains about 25 kcal and virtually no fat.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Mustard greens contain glucosinolates that may affect thyroid function when consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Allergy to cruciferous vegetables
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to Brassicaceae foods.

items.title: Food interactions
items.content: High intake can interfere with iodine absorption, so people with iodine deficiency should consume them in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add mustard greens to soups, stews, omelets, or serve as a side dish. The frozen product can be quickly reheated in a skillet or microwave without added oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen greens at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once thawed, use within 2–3 days and do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Popsicle, No Sugar Added is a frozen dessert made from fruit puree and natural sweeteners, containing no added sugar. It offers a bright fruit flavor, light texture, and is suitable for those monitoring sugar intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popsicles first appeared in the United States in the early 20th century as a way to preserve seasonal fruits.
Sugar‑free versions often use stevia or erythritol, providing sweetness without raising glycemia.
In Russia these products gained popularity after 2015 amid the “healthy eating” trend.
Popsicles are easy to transport and do not require refrigeration until they are frozen.
Flavors range from berry to tropical, depending on the fruits used.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The absence of added sugar helps maintain stable blood glucose levels, beneficial for people prone to diabetes.

items.title: Rich in vitamins C and A
items.content: The fruit base retains vitamin C and provitamin A, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fruit fibers aid digestion and promote a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low‑calorie dessert
items.content: Without sugar and with a light base, the product is less caloric than traditional ice creams.

items.title: No artificial colorings
items.content: Typically colored only with natural fruit pigments, reducing the risk of allergic reactions.

items.title: Allergy to fruit components
items.content: Some individuals may react to specific fruits used in the formulation.

items.title: Presence of artificial sweeteners
items.content: Although sugar‑free sweeteners are considered safe, sensitive people may experience gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Improper storage temperature
items.content: If the product thaws and refreezes, texture and taste can deteriorate.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Acidic fruits may contribute to tooth enamel erosion with frequent consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the popsicle straight from the freezer, blend it into a smoothie, or use it as a refreshing post‑workout snack. For extra flair, top with berries or nuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once removed from the package, consume within 2–3 days to preserve texture and flavor.

pretzels-soft-ready-to-eat-topped-with-m.title: Soft Pretzels, Ready‑to‑Eat, Topped with Meat

content.title: About
content.content: Soft ready‑to‑eat pretzels topped with a savory meat coating are a yeasted dough snack finished with a flavorful meat sauce. The pretzels have a tender, slightly chewy texture and a rich meaty taste, making them a convenient snack for fans of salty bites.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soft pretzels originated in the United States in the early 1920s as a milder alternative to the traditional crunchy version.
The meat topping is usually made from beef or pork seasoned with paprika, garlic, and a blend of spices.
Pretzels are traditionally shaped in a “twist” or “8” to ensure even baking.
In the U.S., soft pretzels are often served with cheese dip, but the meat‑topped version is gaining popularity among protein‑focused eaters.
Some recipes add cheese directly into the dough, creating an even richer bite.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The meat topping provides a substantial amount of complete protein needed for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Combined carbohydrates from the dough and fats in the meat deliver quick, sustained energy, useful before workouts.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat supplies B1, B2, B3, and B6 vitamins that support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Iron, zinc, and phosphorus are present, contributing to blood health and bone strength.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The mix of protein and complex carbs helps keep you feeling full for longer periods.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The meat coating often contains a lot of salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat‑based dough can trigger reactions in individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Meat toppings can be high in saturated fats, so moderation is recommended.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Pretzels are calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy straight from the package as a quick snack, or warm in the microwave or oven for a softer texture. They pair well with cheese dip, mustard, or a spicy sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store in the refrigerator to preserve the meat’s freshness. Discard if the product develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice, white, with peas is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of boiled white rice mixed with cooked green peas. It is commonly served in school cafeterias and used as a quick meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The rice‑and‑pea combination provides a more complete amino‑acid profile than rice alone.
The dish is popular in Eastern European and Asian countries as an inexpensive, nutritious option.
Peas add a natural green colour and a subtle sweetness.
The rice is usually pre‑cooked to full tenderness, reducing home‑cooking time.
Packaging often bears the “NS” label (no fat), making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice supplies slowly digestible starches that provide sustained energy.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peas contribute a notable amount of plant‑based protein, beneficial for muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Peas add fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The product is marked “NS” (no fat), fitting low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both rice and peas provide B1, B3 and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Pea allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high GI, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some packages may contain added salt; check the label if you need a low‑sodium product.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to eat straight from the pack. It can be warmed in a microwave or on the stove, and paired with sauces, vegetables or meat for variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place away from direct light. After opening, keep the package tightly sealed to prevent moisture absorption.
